title: CELA 2025: Microsoft Corporate, External and Legal Affairs Reorganisation Memorandum
pub: Internal memorandum to the Microsoft CELA team, 29 June 2021 (9 pp.)
author: Brad Smith

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The memorandum advocates substantial legal-function redesign, cross-company governance and capability building, but frames these around regulatory adaptation, customer needs and societal impact—not jagged legal-AI capability, user expertise or output verification. It therefore offers a materially different rationale and priority for work redesign rather than directly supporting the cluster’s AI-specific proposition.
qs: But one key to success is ensuring that we structure teams  and fill leadership roles based on the mission and strategies we want to pursue.

And it will call   on us to create strong governance models that rely on CELA teams to work with regulators and  coordinate across the company, while engineering and other teams assume direct responsibility for  huge amounts of work that will need to be done.

mo.t: Regulatory institutions: Governance needs implementation markets
Work redesign: Organisation captures more value than access

kp.k: Regulatory expectations drive multiyear expansion of in-house capabilities
kp.d: Smith announces CELA's largest team expansion since 2010 and biggest reorganisation in 20 years, preparing for Microsoft's needs in the middle of the decade. He presents increasing technology regulation as a reason for a bigger budget, faster team growth and multiyear hiring, rather than reporting measured effects of AI on legal employment.
qs: We’re embarking on the largest expansion of our team since 2010 and our biggest re-organization in 20 years.
It will involve substantial new resources, and it’s a major focus of a bigger budget and faster growth for our team.
As an SLT, we’ve looked beyond the next fiscal year in devising our expansion and hiring plans.

kp.k: Expected regulation spans AI and numerous adjacent legal fields
kp.d: Smith anticipates geographically widespread technology regulation extending beyond competition law to responsible AI, privacy, cybersecurity and other fields. He also expects environmental sustainability regulation by the middle of the decade, if not earlier. He attributes regulatory pressure to technology's societal power, concerns about inequality and democracy, declining trust in some countries and economic nationalism.
qs: This includes new privacy, cybersecurity, responsible AI, digital safety, telecommunications, trade, consumer protection, and accessibility regulations.
In addition, we expect to see new environmental sustainability regulations by the middle of the decade, if not before.
Government officials are focused on the tech sector’s power, importance to society, and impact on economic inequality and democracy itself.

kp.k: Adaptation takes priority over resistance to regulation
kp.d: Smith advocates adapting to regulation while acknowledging its risks, drawing on Microsoft's experience with Windows antitrust obligations. He cites Windows 11 changes, an EU data boundary, cybersecurity support and a French cloud initiative as examples of proactive adaptation. These are management's examples and strategic arguments, not an independent evaluation of regulatory compliance.
qs: There are real risks, and they need a fair hearing. But as a company, we will continue to be more focused on adapting to regulation than fighting against it.
While change is never easy, we believe it’s possible to adapt to new rules and innovate successfully and responsibly.
These include a second app store for Android apps supported by Amazon and the ability for developers to "bring their own commerce engine" and keep 100 percent of their revenue.

kp.k: Legal coordination accompanies distributed responsibility for compliance
kp.d: The proposed governance model assigns CELA regulator engagement and company-wide coordination while engineering and other teams directly undertake substantial implementation work. Smith's stated goal is to build capabilities before new laws take effect, allowing compliance from their implementation date while preserving rapid innovation.
qs: We will need to build a capability across Microsoft that enables us both to comply with global regulations and innovate quickly.

And it will call on us to create strong governance models that rely on CELA teams to work with regulators and coordinate across the company, while engineering and other teams assume direct responsibility for huge amounts of work that will need to be done.
Our goal is to build our regulatory capabilities ahead of the adoption of new laws, thereby ensuring we can comply fully the day their implementation day arrives.

kp.k: Customized technology solutions require deeper legal involvement
kp.d: Smith argues that customer relationships must move beyond standardized offerings toward customized solutions informed by customers' businesses, goals and needs. Closer engineering–sales collaboration changes legal teams' work because these solutions involve intellectual property, data, privacy and industry-specific regulatory requirements. He expects this trend to intensify between 2021 and the middle of the decade.
qs: No longer is it sufficient to simply provide standardized products and services. Instead, we must create customized solutions.
Engineering and sales teams now work closely together as we design specific customer solutions.

Customized solutions need to take account of important intellectual property, data, and privacy issues. They must also reflect regulatory requirements that are often specific to a customer’s industry.
All this will increase even further between now and the middle of the decade.

kp.k: Customers' AI use broadens Microsoft's legal support mission
kp.d: Smith predicts that responsible AI, privacy and cybersecurity regulation will cover technology use in other industries as well as technology suppliers. He frames helping customers use technology responsibly and legally as an increasingly important dimension of Microsoft's mission; the memorandum does not describe AI automating this legal work.
qs: Many technology regulations – such as for privacy, cybersecurity, and responsible AI – will apply not only to tech companies but to the use of technology by other industries as well.
Our mission of empowering others therefore will take on an added dimension; more than ever it will involve helping customers use technology in a responsible and legally proper way.

kp.k: Regulatory teams consolidate AI governance and security responsibilities
kp.d: The announced structure concentrates most regulatory work in two growing teams. Julie Brill's Privacy and Regulatory Affairs team receives responsible AI, digital safety, accessibility compliance and a new regulatory governance role. Tom Burt's Customer Security and Trust team receives telecommunications regulation and expanded investment for cybersecurity work, including nation-state attacks, ransomware and lawful data access.
qs: We will align most of CELA’s regulatory work in two growing teams under established leaders.
In addition, we are moving the teams for responsible AI, digital safety, accessibility compliance, and a new regulatory governance role into this team.

The team’s continuing mission is to help strengthen cybersecurity protection for our customers, with expanded and consolidated work to address nation-state attacks, fight ransomware threats, and ensure appropriate lawful access to data.
we are moving to CST the team that addresses telecommunications regulations, which has been in PRA.

kp.k: Legal restructuring integrates customer support and corporate specialties
kp.d: Smith announces two new general counsel-led groups. Lisa Tanzi's Customer Experience & Policy team integrates CELA support for engineering and go-to-market groups, including teams in 54 countries. Hossein Nowbar's Corporate Legal Affairs team combines intellectual property, litigation, compliance, competition and support for corporate functions. The stated rationale is deeper customer solutions alongside regulatory and societal priorities.
qs: Lisa Tanzi is being promoted to General Counsel, leading a new Customer Experience & Policy (CxP) team.
combine and integrate the CELA groups that support all the engineering and go-to-market groups across Microsoft, including our teams located in 54 countries around the world.
Hossein Nowbar is being promoted to General Counsel and Corporate Secretary for a new Corporate Legal Affairs (CLA) team.

This will combine our corporate legal groups, including our intellectual property, litigation, compliance, and competition teams, as well as the teams that support corporate functions such as HR plus Finance and BD.

kp.k: Production platforms frame the customer empowerment strategy
kp.d: Reporting Satya's distinction, Smith separates technologies used as production inputs from distribution mechanisms that match supply and demand. He reports Satya's view that production technologies contribute most to broadly beneficial growth, while distribution technologies are beneficial conditionally on market makers not capturing all surplus. Smith positions Microsoft predominantly on the production side and connects that orientation to customer independence.
qs: The first set of digital technologies are “factors of production” and are inputs that are used by customers to create more products and services.
Then there are “factors of distribution” which play a role in matching supply and demand and driving efficiencies for the participants.
But as Satya has said, “factors of production” are the most important in driving economic growth that is broadly beneficial.

And “factors of distribution” are also beneficial if the market maker does not enrich itself with all the surplus created at the expense of customers and suppliers in otherwise competitive marketplaces.
We want customers to become independent with us, not dependent on us.

kp.k: Societal technology ambitions reshape CELA's broader responsibilities
kp.d: Smith presents digital technology, data and AI as potential contributors to solving major societal problems, citing COVID-19 experience and opportunities in climate, humanitarian relief and racial equity. The reorganisation makes Environmental Sustainability a direct report to Smith and expands Technology and Corporate Responsibility's democracy, disinformation, journalism, justice reform and racial equity work. These are strategic opportunities and announced responsibilities, not measured AI outcomes.
qs: In the world today, if there’s a big problem, there is probably an opportunity for digital technology, data, and artificial intelligence to be part of the solution.
We have an even bigger opportunity to deploy technology to address climate change, support humanitarian relief efforts, and advance racial equity.

Lucas Joppa will continue to lead our Environmental Sustainability (ES) team but will now report to me directly, reflecting the increasing importance of sustainability and its growing connection with virtually everything we do.
It will also add to its work relating to justice reform and racial equity, while taking on new and critical work to advance and protect democracy.

kp.k: Nonprofit support combines commercial delivery and philanthropic reinvestment
kp.d: Smith describes Technology for Social Impact as a Microsoft Philanthropies team combining donations, sales and technology support. Its growth in contribution margin is reinvested into donations and team resources. The memorandum announces substantial additional investment in this team and expanded digital skilling, illustrating the broader service-delivery responsibilities within CELA rather than a legal-services pricing model.
qs: As part of Microsoft Philanthropies, this expanding team combines donations, sales, and technology support under one roof.
And with its unique business model, we reinvest its growth in contribution margin back into philanthropic donations and expanded resources for the team.

Kate Behncken will continue to lead Microsoft Philanthropies as we expand its work, including substantially investing additional resources in the Technology for Social Impact team, supporting its growing business and strengthening our support for nonprofit organizations around the world.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Brad Smith predicts that responsible-AI regulation, alongside other technology regulation, will expand Microsoft's legal and customer-support responsibilities.
pts.d: Smith anticipates that technology regulation will govern both technology suppliers and customers' uses of technology. Combined with a shift toward customized customer solutions, this will require Microsoft's legal teams to address intellectual property, data, privacy and industry-specific regulatory requirements and help customers use technology lawfully. This is a claim about AI-related compliance demand and changes to in-house legal work, not a claim that AI automates or replaces lawyers.

pts.k: Smith announces expanded regulatory capacity and the integration of responsible AI into Microsoft's Privacy and Regulatory Affairs team.
pts.d: Smith presents investment, hiring, organizational consolidation and cross-company governance as necessary responses to anticipated global technology regulation. Responsible AI is explicitly included in the reorganization, but the wider budget and headcount expansion is not attributed to AI alone. CELA will work with regulators and coordinate compliance, while engineering and other teams will have direct implementation responsibilities.

pts.k: In the memorandum's broader technology-policy domain, Smith claims that AI, data and digital technology can contribute to solving major societal problems.
pts.d: Smith identifies pandemic response as an experienced example and anticipates greater opportunities in climate change, humanitarian relief and racial equity. The prediction concerns technology collectively; the memorandum does not identify particular AI systems, isolate AI's contribution or claim specific measured outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Smith grounds the legal-work and organizational claims in executive planning, stakeholder consultation, regulatory observations and Microsoft's operating experience.
pts.d: The memorandum reports three months of leadership planning and consultation with internal and external stakeholders. Smith invokes experience adapting to antitrust rules and working closely with customers during the pandemic. These are the offered experiential and strategic bases for the predictions, rather than AI-specific research findings. The announced responsible-AI team transfer is a concrete organizational commitment. The societal-benefit claim rests on a general reference to pandemic experience, without named AI deployments, quantitative results or benchmarks.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The principal planning horizon is June 2021 to the middle of the decade, with budget and headcount expansion over the following 18 months.
pts.d: Smith frames CELA 2025 as a four-year effort rather than a one-year capability build. Regulatory readiness is intended to precede new laws' implementation. The legal-work predictions depend on expanding, jurisdictionally varied technology regulation and growing demand for customized customer solutions. The societal AI claim is qualified as an opportunity to be part of a solution, not a guarantee that AI will solve these problems.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are Microsoft's in-house legal and regulatory teams, engineering and sales teams, and customers across regulated industries; the broader technology claims concern public and nonprofit beneficiaries.
pts.d: CELA faces expanded compliance coordination and customer-facing legal responsibilities. Responsible-AI personnel move into Privacy and Regulatory Affairs, while engineering and other teams undertake implementation work. Customers outside the technology sector are expected to face regulation of their technology use and need more tailored legal and technical support. The broader societal claims concern people affected by climate change, humanitarian crises and racial inequity, with nonprofit organizations identified as important delivery partners. The memorandum makes no specific prediction about law-firm staffing, ALSPs, legal fees or AI-driven displacement.
